items.q: What is an index? What index data structures exist and what are they used for?
items.a:
Index = an auxiliary structure that finds data fast without a full scan.

[[o:Trade-off]]: costs storage + slows down writes (index must be updated).

**Index families:**
- [[b:B+Tree]]: default RDBMS — equality + range + sort
- [[b:Hash]]: O(1) equality, useless for range/sort
- [[b:LSM-tree]]: sequential writes (Cassandra, RocksDB) — write-heavy
- [[b:Bitmap]]: low-cardinality columns in a data warehouse
- [[b:Inverted index]]: full-text search (Elasticsearch/Lucene)
- [[b:GiST/GIN]] (Postgres): JSONB, full-text, geo

:::tip Bottom line
there is no 'best' index — pick based on [[g:access pattern]]. B+Tree is the most balanced choice for OLTP.
:::

:::deep
- every index slows down INSERT/UPDATE and costs storage (write amplification) → [[r:don't index carelessly]]; weigh the read/write ratio
- OTA: the `booking` table needs a composite B+Tree for history; searching flights/destinations uses Elasticsearch (inverted); 'seats remaining' can use a bitmap/partial index

Bottom line: 'there's no best index, only an index that fits the pattern.'
:::

items.q: The B+Tree algorithm: why is lookup O(log n), and what are page split and fanout?
items.a: B+Tree is balanced: every leaf sits at the same depth. - each node = 1 page (e.g. 16KB in InnoDB) holding many keys → [[g:very large fanout]] (hundreds) - the tree is only [[g:3–4 levels]] deep for millions/billions of rows → a lookup takes only a few page reads - data lives at the leaves; leaves are chained into a linked list → [[g:range scans are cheap]] **Page split:** when an insert fills a page, it splits in two → costs I/O + causes fragmentation. - inserting *sequential* keys (auto-increment) → limits splits - inserting random keys (UUID v4) → [[r:splits everywhere]] :::tip Bottom line 'short tree + high fanout + linked leaves' is why B+Tree is fast for both point lookups and range queries. A sequential PK avoids splits. ::: :::deep **Quantifying it:** a 16KB InnoDB page, BIGINT PK 8B + pointer 6B → fanout ~1000. - 3 levels ≈ 1000³ = 1 billion keys → every data point is ~3 page reads from the root (upper levels are usually already in the buffer pool) - this is why adding an index turns a scan of millions of rows into a handful of page accesses [[r:Write amplification]]: every secondary index adds extra writes on INSERT/UPDATE and can trigger page splits → a table with many indexes writes noticeably slower. - random keys (UUIDv4) → splits and fragmentation drive down the buffer pool hit ratio (measure with `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS`) - comparing B+Tree (good reads) vs LSM (good writes) is a great closing point :::

items.q: What's the difference between a clustered and a secondary index in InnoDB? What are the consequences for choosing a PK?
items.a: - [[b:Clustered index]] = the PK; leaves hold *the entire row* (one per table) - [[b:Secondary index]]: leaves hold the indexed value + the *PK* → after looking up the secondary index you must [[o:'lookback']] to the clustered index for the remaining columns **Consequences for choosing a PK:** a short, sequential PK (BIGINT auto-increment) beats a random UUID because: - every secondary index stores the PK → a long PK [[r:bloats every index]] - a UUID causes page splits If you must use a UUID, consider [[g:UUIDv7]] (time-ordered). :::deep - since secondary indexes store the PK: the bigger the PK, the more every secondary index bloats → costs buffer pool RAM, lowers the hit ratio; changing a PK value is extremely expensive → [[o:a PK should be immutable]] - OTA: the `booking` table is queried heavily by `(user_id, created_at)` → a covering index `(user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (status, pnr)` (Postgres) so 'booking history' doesn't need a lookback - when the optimizer would have to look back too many rows, it may abandon the index for a full scan → a covering index saves p99 :::

items.q: Composite index (a,b,c): leftmost-prefix rule and covering index?
items.a:
Index `(a,b,c)` can be used for [[g:leftmost prefix]]:
- `a`, `a,b`, `a,b,c`, or `a + range(b)`
- [[r:NOT]] for `b` alone or `b,c`
- after a range column, the columns that follow can no longer filter

[[g:Covering index]]: contains every column the query needs (including SELECT) → `Using index`, no lookback.

Column order: [[o:equality columns first, range/sort columns after]].

:::deep
- Postgres uses `INCLUDE` to add non-key columns to the leaf (covering without growing the key)
- OTA: `(user_id, status, created_at)` serves 'a user's active bookings over time'; add `INCLUDE(pnr, amount)` so the list doesn't need a lookback → saves p99

Nuance: MySQL 8.0+ has *index skip scan*, which can sometimes use (a,b,c) for a condition only on b when a has low cardinality — but [[r:don't rely on it]], still design around leftmost. MySQL 8 also has *descending indexes* for mixed-direction ORDER BY.
:::

items.q: In which cases does an index NOT get used even though the column has one?
items.a:
'Has an index' [[r:≠]] 'index gets used'. Cases where the index is skipped:
- a function/expression on the column: `WHERE YEAR(d)=2026` (rewrite as a range, or use a functional index)
- leading wildcard `LIKE '%x'`
- implicit type conversion (a string column compared to a number, mismatched collation) — a trap with string-typed account codes
- low selectivity (a boolean column) → the optimizer picks a full scan
- `OR` across different indexed columns; `!=`/`NOT IN` over a large set

[[g:Always verify with EXPLAIN.]]

:::deep
**Five common production traps:**
- [[r:OR]] can sometimes be rescued by *index merge* but usually performs worse than a `UNION ALL` of two separately indexed queries
- [[r:IN (...) that's too large]] → the optimizer switches to a full scan
- [[r:sort/group order that doesn't match the index order]] → `Using filesort`
- [[r:skewed statistics]] after loading a large batch of data → the optimizer mis-estimates → run `ANALYZE TABLE`
- [[r:parameter sniffing]]/plan cache picking a bad plan for a skewed-distribution value

Final verdict: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to compare actual rows vs estimated — a large gap means bad statistics or column correlation.
:::

items.q: How do selectivity and cardinality affect the optimizer's decisions?
items.a:
- [[b:Cardinality]] = number of distinct values
- [[b:Selectivity]] = cardinality/total rows (closer to 1 = 'filters more strongly')

The optimizer uses these statistics to estimate row counts → picks an index/plan.
- stale/skewed statistics → picks a bad plan → run `ANALYZE TABLE` to refresh
- a low-selectivity column is less useful to index on its own

:::deep
- the optimizer relies on histograms/statistics to estimate row counts, then picks the index/join order/method
- *stale/skewed* statistics (after a bulk load, after a large delete) → picks a bad full scan or nested-loop → `ANALYZE` (Postgres)/`ANALYZE TABLE` (MySQL)
- a skewed-distribution column (`status='SUCCESS'` at 99%) needs a [[g:histogram]] so the optimizer knows 'SUCCESS' isn't selective while 'FAILED' is
- *parameter sniffing*/plan cache keeps the plan that's optimal for this value but bad for another → monitor estimated vs actual rows (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`)
:::

items.q: The 4 isolation levels and their corresponding anomalies? MySQL vs Postgres defaults?
items.a:
LevelPreventsRemaining anomaly
READ UNCOMMITTED—dirty read
READ COMMITTEDdirtynon-repeatable + phantom (default PG/Oracle)
REPEATABLE READ+ non-repeatablephantom (InnoDB blocks it via next-key)
SERIALIZABLEevery anomalymost expensive
- [[b:dirty]] = reading something not yet committed - [[b:non-repeatable]] = re-reading a row and getting a different value - [[b:phantom]] = re-reading a set and getting a different row count Default: [[o:MySQL = RR]], [[o:Postgres/Oracle = RC]]. :::deep - RC (PG/Oracle) takes a new snapshot per statement → sees the latest committed data but is non-repeatable within a tx - RR (MySQL/InnoDB) snapshots once for the whole tx; InnoDB also blocks phantoms with next-key locks on a *locking read* - SERIALIZABLE is expensive (predicate locks/aborts) Going deeper for fintech: most money-moving logic runs at [[g:RC/RR + deliberate row locks]] (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` / conditional update) for contention hotspots, instead of raising isolation globally (expensive + more deadlocks). Choose isolation [[o:per transaction]], don't flip on SERIALIZABLE 'just to be safe'. :::

items.q: MVCC in InnoDB, and why doesn't MySQL's RR suffer phantoms the way the ANSI standard predicts?
items.a: Every row has a `trx_id` + `roll_pointer` pointing into the undo log (older versions). On read, InnoDB builds a [[g:read view]] to pick the visible version: - [[b:RR]]: builds the read view *once*, at the first SELECT (a consistent snapshot for the whole tx) - [[b:RC]]: rebuilds it on every statement **Phantoms:** - a plain SELECT → already immune thanks to the snapshot - a locking read (`FOR UPDATE`, INSERT/UPDATE) → [[g:next-key lock]] locks the gap itself, blocking new rows from being inserted into the range :::tip Bottom line InnoDB's RR prevents phantoms via snapshot reads (plain reads) + gap/next-key locks (locking reads). A notable difference from the ANSI standard. ::: :::deep - a read view holds `m_ids` (active trxs), `min/max_trx_id`, `creator_trx_id`; a version is visible if the transaction that created it committed *before* the view was captured - older versions live in the undo log; undo is only *purged* once no read view still needs it [[r:Trap]]: a transaction left open too long (a report running for 30 minutes at RR) blocks purging → undo bloats, the history list grows long, dragging down performance. - Postgres stores tuple versions directly in the table → needs `VACUUM` to clean up dead tuples; autovacuum falling behind → 'table bloat' - operationally: [[g:avoid long-running reads on the primary]]; push them to a replica/snapshot :::

items.q: Record / gap / next-key locks, and optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
items.a:
**Lock types (InnoDB):** - [[b:Record lock]]: locks an index record - [[b:Gap lock]]: locks the gap between records (prevents inserts → prevents phantoms) - [[b:Next-key]] = record + gap **Pessimistic vs Optimistic:** - [[b:Pessimistic]] (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`): locks immediately — fits high contention (e.g. hot inventory/balance) - [[b:Optimistic]] (a version column): no lock, retry on conflict — fits low contention/distributed systems 
UPDATE account SET balance=balance-?, version=version+1
WHERE id=? AND version=?;  -- 0 rows => retry
:::deep - gap locks only apply at REPEATABLE READ, not at READ COMMITTED (so RC deadlocks less but allows phantoms) - [[r:a subtle source of deadlocks]]: a missing index forces `UPDATE ... WHERE` to scan and place a next-key lock over a large range → adding an index to narrow the locked range is a non-obvious way to 'reduce deadlocks' [[o:Hot row]] contention that's extremely high (e.g. a shared promotion voucher): both optimistic and pessimistic approaches choke → architectural solutions: - [[g:shard the balance]] (split it into N sub-accounts that sum together) - or funnel through a *sequential per-account queue* - Why the `version` column usually lives on the aggregate root rather than being scattered across tables: the aggregate is the natural unit for optimistic locking (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q2). :::

items.q: Deadlocks: how do they happen, how does InnoDB handle them, and how do you prevent them?
items.a:
[[r:Deadlock]] = two transactions locking in opposite order, waiting on each other in a cycle.

InnoDB *detects the cycle* (wait-for graph) and rolls back the transaction with the cheaper undo cost (error 1213); check `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS`.

**Prevention:**
- lock in a [[g:consistent order]] (always lock the smaller id first) — eliminates most transfer-style deadlocks
- keep transactions short; don't make network calls or wait on the user while holding a lock
- good indexes so fewer rows get locked (missing index → gap locks spread wide)
- prepare for [[g:idempotent retries]] at the app layer

:::deep
InnoDB rolls back the victim with the cheaper undo cost (error 1213); check the LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section.

**Four ways to reduce deadlocks:**
- [[g:lock in a consistent order]] (lock the smaller account id first — eliminates the A→B vs B→A transfer deadlock)
- keep transactions short, no network calls/waiting on the user while holding a lock
- [[g:good indexes]] so fewer rows get locked (missing index → next-key locks spread over a wide range, more deadlocks)
- [[g:idempotent retries]] at the app layer (deadlocks are normal under high concurrency)

Going deeper for OTA: transferring money/exchanging tickets between two accounts must order its locks; seat-hold uses a conditional update (doesn't hold a lock for long).

- The same problem at the application layer: dining philosophers, the 4 Coffman conditions, and ordering resources to break the wait cycle (23-java-concurrency-coding.classic-synchronisation-problems.q3).
:::

items.q: Reading EXPLAIN: which columns to check first? What are the warning signs that something needs optimizing?
items.a:
**Columns to check first:**
- [[b:type]]: const > eq_ref > ref > range > index > ALL ([[r:ALL on a large table = red flag]])
- [[b:key]]: the index actually used (NULL = none used)
- [[b:rows]]: estimated rows scanned
- [[b:Extra]]: `Using index` (covering, good); `Using filesort`/`Using temporary` = expensive, needs optimizing

Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (MySQL 8) to get real execution timings.

:::tip In practice
grab a real query from RDS pre-prod, run EXPLAIN, and be able to say 'rows went from 2M to 1.2k after adding an index' — far more convincing than theory alone.
:::

:::deep
- `rows` estimate way off from reality (EXPLAIN ANALYZE) → wrong statistics/column correlation
- `Using temporary; Using filesort` on a pagination query → revisit the index for ORDER BY, switch to keyset pagination
- `type=index` (full index scan) on a large table → the index isn't selective enough
- Postgres: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows shared hit/read (real I/O)

Tip: save a good plan as a baseline; when p99 spikes, diff the plans to catch a [[r:plan regression]].

- One level deeper — `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`: estimated vs actual rows, and what `loops` and `buffers` tell you (18-query-optimization.measure-first-reading-the-execution-plan.q2).
:::

items.q: What common query optimization techniques exist beyond indexing?
items.a:
Beyond indexing:
- [[r:avoid `SELECT *`]] (reads extra columns + breaks covering)
- keyset pagination instead of a large OFFSET
- batch instead of looping queries
- avoid functions on WHERE columns
- rewrite correlated subqueries as JOINs/window functions
- deliberate denormalization for read-heavy paths
- covering indexes; partitioning for pruning
- push heavy aggregation to a replica/OLAP

[[g:Always measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE + the slow query log.]]

:::warn Interview trap
Rattling off a list of techniques is a mid-level answer. A senior-level answer starts with *measuring*: which query dominates total time according to `pg_stat_statements`, what its plan looks like, and only then picking a technique. A 200ms query that runs once an hour isn't worth touching, while a 20ms query running 5000 times a second is the real culprit — getting this backwards is the most common mistake.
:::

:::deep
- measurement tools: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` + slow query log + `pg_stat_statements`
- OTA: a search/pricing screen with extremely heavy reads → [[g:cache + a dedicated read model]] (lightweight CQRS) instead of optimizing each query against the transactional table

Principle: [[o:measure first, optimize whatever takes the most time, don't guess]].

:::

items.q: LSM-tree vs B+Tree — why do write-heavy databases choose LSM?
items.a:
B+TreeLSM-tree
Writein-place (random I/O)memtable → SSTable (sequential)
Readfastslower (many SSTables + bloom filter)
StrengthOLTP, read-heavywrite-heavy, time-series
Used inMySQL/PostgresCassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB
:::deep - LSM writes into a memtable (RAM) → flushes to an immutable SSTable (sequential write) → background *compaction* merges them - [[g:Benefit]]: high write throughput (sequential), good compression - [[r:Cost]]: *read amplification* (offset by bloom filters), *write & space amplification* from compaction (background CPU/I/O, can spike latency) - tunable: size-tiered vs leveled compaction (trades off read vs space) OTA: high-volume logs/clickstream/audit trails suit LSM well; the transaction ledger still uses an RDBMS B+Tree. :::
